title: The Tip That Steers the Axon

scenes.visual: Title card: The Tip That Steers the Axon.

scenes.tts: A growing axon has to find one partner among many cells. The work is done at its tip, a moving fan called the growth cone. The growth cone feels its way. Molecules around it, called guidance cues, attract it or repel it. When a cue reaches one side more strongly, the growth cone turns. Turn by turn, it steers the axon to its target. So how does a tip move, and how does it turn?
scenes.visual: Wide view of an axon crossing a field of cells; its fan-shaped tip bends toward a green attractive cloud and away from a red repellent cloud, then reaches a target cell.

scenes.tts: First, the evidence. Gundersen and Barrett placed a pipette releasing nerve growth factor near the axons of chick sensory neurons. The side of each growth cone nearer the pipette met more of it, and the growth cones turned toward it. Campbell and Holt then cut growth cones from frog retinal neurons away from their cell bodies. The isolated tips still turned to guidance cues. The decision is made at the tip.
scenes.visual: A pipette beside a growth cone with a shaded gradient, darker on the near side; the cone bends toward it. Then a cut line across the axon behind the cone; the freed tip still bends toward a cue.

scenes.tts: Now open the fan. Microtubules fill its centre. Actin fills the edge, and the actin is never still. New actin joins the filaments at the front. Motor proteins called myosin two pull the whole network back toward the centre. That backward movement is retrograde flow. If actin is added at the front and carried back at the same rate, the edge goes nowhere. The engine runs, but the car stays put.
scenes.visual: Top-down fan with purple microtubules in the centre and teal actin at the edge; slice to a side view; teal new actin enters at the front, red flow arrows carry it back, a marker shows the edge not moving.
scenes.narration: Now open the fan. Microtubules fill its centre. Actin fills the edge, and the actin is never still. New actin joins the filaments at the front. Motor proteins called myosin II pull the whole network back toward the centre. That backward movement is retrograde flow. If actin is added at the front and carried back at the same rate, the edge goes nowhere. The engine runs, but the car stays put.

scenes.tts: Now add a clutch. When adhesion molecules link the actin network to the surface under it, retrograde flow slows, and the same actin addition pushes the edge forward. Tim Mitchison and Marc Kirschner proposed this in 1988. Put it as a rule. The rate of advance equals the rate of actin addition, minus the rate of retrograde flow.
scenes.visual: Yellow adhesion links appear under the network; the red flow arrows shorten and the edge crosses the marker; the equation builds in colour beside three bars for addition, flow and advance.

scenes.tts: Turning is that rule, applied unequally. A cue on one side shifts actin assembly, flow or adhesion there, so one side advances more than the other. Drugs released onto one side give simple results. Remove actin on one side, and the growth cone turns away from that side.
scenes.visual: Top-down growth cone with a green advance arrow on each side; a cue on the left lengthens the left arrow and the path bends left. Then actin is cleared on one side and the cone bends away from it.

scenes.tts: Microtubules steer too. Stabilize them on one side, and the growth cone turns toward that side. Break them down on one side, and it turns away. As the edge moves, microtubules extend into the new territory, the fan behind them narrows, and that stretch becomes axon shaft. Keep the rule. The tip senses a cue, and turning is the difference between its two sides.
scenes.visual: A pipette marked taxol on one side; purple microtubules invade that side and the cone bends toward it. Then microtubules fill the new stretch and the fan narrows into shaft; the closing line is written: senses a cue, turns by the difference between sides.
